not_covered: In New York, 128 tracts gentrified, which was the highest raw total among cities reviewed [Source: ev-2].
Economic disparities have intensified significantly across metropolitan areas. [Source: ev-1]
Several metros exhibit extreme patterns where income ratios reach 18:1 between top and bottom earners [Source: ev-1].
Specifically, Atlanta and Washington D.C. [Source: ev-1]
Housing affordability has deteriorated as costs outpaced wage growth. [Source: ev-1]
On an inflation-adjusted basis, incomes rose just 8.5%, whereas home prices rose more than 56% [Source: ev-4].
The national price-to-income ratio is approximately 4.6–4.7 [Source: ev-1] [Source: ev-4].
In California cities such as Los Angeles, San Jose, Long Beach, San Francisco, and San Diego, ratios range from 9.6 to 12.2—more than double the national average [Source: ev-1] [Source: ev-4].
Five of the six large U.S. [Source: ev-1]
cities with the highest price-to-income ratios are in California [Source: ev-4].
Demographic shifts have accompanied these economic changes. [Source: ev-1]

Gentrifying neighborhoods saw population increases (+6.5%) and became whiter (non-Hispanic white share increased by +4.3 percentage points), while poverty rates decreased by 0.7 percentage points [Source: ev-1] [Source: ev-2].

In contrast, lower-income areas that did not gentrify experienced slight population losses (-2.4%), an increase in minority concentration, and a rise in poverty of 6.7 percentage points [Source: ev-1] [Source: ev-2].

Displacement patterns vary by race; residents from historically Black gentrifying neighborhoods tend to move to poorer non-gentrifying areas, whereas residents from other gentrifying areas often move to wealthier ones [Source: ev-1].
Since 1980, nearly 80% of the country's under-45 population growth was concentrated in metro areas with over 1 million residents [Source: ev-1] [ev-4].
